newsitem.title: UK: Salvors attack insurers' plans to alter contracts.
newsitem.headline: Salvors attack insurers' plans to alter contracts.

text.p: The International Salvage Union (ISU) has attacked proposals being considered by P&I insurers to change the way salvage contracts are awarded and operated.

ISU executive committee member and group director of maritime contracting for Smit Internationale NV Hans Walenkamp said in London on Wednesday that proposals being considered by the P&I Clubs would accelerate the decline of the salvage industry.

Speaking at the first International Marine Salvage Conference he said: "Proposals have been prepared which call for the complete abandonment of existing arrangements for the provision of salvage and pollution prevention services".

Walenkamp said adoption of the system proposed by "certain interests within the P&I community" were an attempt by the cargo insurers to win control of salvage operations and minimise their exposure to environmental claims.
"The new salvage industry would lack open competition and the ability to generate worthwhile earnings. It would no longer be in charge of its own destiny," he said.
"How do we stop the rot when the decline of the salvage industry accelerates as a result of this reform?" he asked.
Walenkamp said the P&I Clubs were planning to appoint three or four lead salvors representing various regions. They would draw upon other salvors' resources for particular operations.
"Every salvage would be overseen by the Club's representative or consultant. All work would be performed under daily hire terms," he said.
Walenkamp added that such moves would mean the end of the accepted Lloyd's Open Form (LOF) system with its no cure-no pay principle.

The ISU accepts that reform of LOF is required but salvors claim the no cure-no pay principle promotes immediate action by deferring commercial issues until after salvage is achieved and encourages successful completion of operations.
International Group of P&I Clubs salvage sub-committee member Colin Williams responded that the mutual cargo insurers were investigating "improvements, not replacement" of the existing regime.

Williams, who is also associate manager with the Steamship Mutual Underwriting Association, said the International Group was considering a radical proposal for the Clubs to cover risks and pay daily rates, but that it was one of several possible ideas which have not yet been approved.

"The plan would be open to all owners and salvors with the proviso that they would not be able to cherry-pick the response which would pay best. The enhanced daily rate system might therefore make responses quicker," Williams said.
He countered claims that the Clubs had only a minority interest in the cost of salvage contracts and said their involvement was steady rising.
Williams also said the number of LOF contracts being used was falling all the time because the system was becoming slow and costly to administrate.
-- Paul Berrill, Reuters Shipping News + Tel 171 542 4087
